column5: Joseph's prison cupbearer dream; grapes pressed into Pharaoh's cup
column6: The commentary's imprisoned cupbearer dreams of pressing grapes and serving wine; Genesis gives the same prison dream in which the cupbearer squeezes grapes into Pharaoh's cup, a direct scene parallel.

column5: Cupbearer forgets Joseph
column6: The commentary says the cupbearer forgets Joseph after his release, leaving Joseph in prison; Genesis likewise says the restored cupbearer did not remember Joseph, making the delay part of the shared story.

column5: Two-year delay before Pharaoh's dreams
column6: The commentary makes delayed recollection lengthen Joseph's imprisonment; Genesis marks two full years before Pharaoh dreams and the cupbearer remembers, giving that wait a measured duration.

column5: Cupbearer recalls his failure
column6: The commentary's freed cupbearer remembers Joseph only after a long interval; Genesis has him recall his failure before Pharaoh and recount Joseph's prison interpretation, ending the forgotten interval.

column5: Surplus stored in the cities
column6: The commentary links Joseph's seven abundant years with preserving grain for scarcity; Genesis says Joseph gathers the produce of those years and stores food in the cities, the same plan of holding yield through time.

column5: End of the years of plenty
column6: The commentary orders Joseph's story as abundance, hard years, then renewed yield; Genesis says the seven years of plenty end, marking the same turn in the agricultural calendar.

column5: Famine follows abundance
column6: The commentary's stored grain is for the years of hardship; Genesis says famine begins and the land still has food in Egypt, showing the preserved yield surviving the time of loss.

column5: Stored grain released beyond Egypt
column6: The commentary's final Joseph year restores productive pressing after scarcity; Genesis has all lands come to Egypt to buy grain, showing stored abundance flowing outward when famine arrives.

column5: Oath and exclusion from the sworn land
column6: The commentary places an oath just before a verdict of loss; Numbers says the rebellious generation will not see the land sworn to their ancestors, joining oath, missed inheritance, and a closed future.

column5: Caleb as the exception
column6: After the generation is excluded, Numbers singles out Caleb, who followed fully and will enter the land; this gives a precise biblical instance of a general loss followed by an exception for the faithful.

column5: A thousand years as a day and night watch
column6: The commentary holds a long era and a short day-part together; the psalm measures a thousand years as yesterday or a night watch, explicitly collapsing vast time into a brief interval.

column5: Morning growth fades by evening
column6: The commentary hears the afternoon as a closing day with dwindling light and a life nearing its end; the psalm describes grass flourishing in the morning and fading by evening, making mortality visible in the daily cycle.

column5: Seventy or eighty years pass quickly
column6: The commentary says the same word can name an era and a person's age; the psalm measures human years at seventy or eighty and says they soon fly, linking a long life to a finite span.

column5: Oath that bars entry into rest
column6: The commentary's opening oath stands at the threshold of a verdict; the psalm ends its warning with God's sworn denial of entry into rest, a close formal and thematic parallel of oath followed by loss.

column5: Merchants impatient for the sacred day to end
column6: The commentary makes the day's closing edge a time when work and opportunity run short; Amos depicts grain sellers asking when the new moon and Sabbath will end so they can trade and falsify measures, turning sacred time into an obstacle to profit.

column5: An oath against those who exploit the poor
column6: The commentary's garden owners swear to keep the poor from their harvest; Amos has the Lord swear not to forget merchants who trample the needy, joining oath, withheld food, and judgment.

column5: Grapes left for the poor
column6: The commentary's garden owners plan to exclude the poor from their crop; Deuteronomy commands leaving remaining grapes for the stranger, orphan, and widow, setting shared yield against total retention.

column5: Withheld grain curses its owner
column6: The commentary contrasts a hand that keeps produce with one that lets its extract become a gift; Proverbs says people curse the one who withholds grain and bless the seller, making the ethical difference between retention and release explicit.

column5: Work while it is day
column6: The commentary hears afternoon as the closing part of the day, when undone work has little time left; Jesus says to do the work while it is day because night comes when no one can work, making the shrinking window explicit.

column5: Pressed measure overflowing as a gift
column6: The commentary makes pressing yield an image of generosity when the extract flows out; Jesus describes a measure pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing into another's lap, a striking image of abundance given away.

column5: A thirsty tongue with no available sip
column6: The commentary's dried tongue and failed rescue-sip image meets the rich man after death asking for a drop of water to cool his tongue; Luke makes relief unavailable after the decisive time has passed.

column5: Fortunes reversed after death
column6: The commentary's withheld garden yield ends in deprivation; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but their conditions are now reversed, making the lost opportunity irreversible.

column5: Full wage for the eleventh-hour workers
column6: The commentary's closing hour warns that little time remains to finish work; Jesus' parable pays those hired at the eleventh hour a full denarius, countering the assumption that a late start must mean a diminished share.

column5: Honi sleeps through seventy years
column6: The commentary links refuge in a cave with sleep that seems brief to the sleepers but spans centuries; Honi sleeps within a rocky shelter for seventy years and wakes into a changed generation, a Jewish time-dislocation parallel.

column4: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 1.95
column5: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
column6: The commentary's cave youths sleep through centuries and wake in a changed age; Gregory recounts the Christian Seven Sleepers of Ephesus in their cave, a direct narrative parallel whose chronology varies among tellings.

column5: Hebrews repeats the oath of exclusion
column6: The commentary frames the oath as the threshold to a verdict of loss; Hebrews quotes Psalm 95's oath that the wilderness generation will not enter God's rest, reading the oath as a warning about salvation and missed time.

column5: Believers enter the promised rest
column6: The commentary moves from loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews interprets the wilderness oath by saying that those who believe enter the rest, giving faith the role of escape from the exclusion.

column5: Midrash explains Joseph's extra prison years
column6: The commentary treats the cupbearer's forgetting as a long delay; Genesis Rabbah reads Joseph's doubled plea to be remembered as the reason for two more years in prison, turning the delay into a lesson about reliance and trust.

column5: Human labor continues until evening
column6: The commentary describes asr as the hour when work is nearly done and remaining time narrows; the psalm says people go out to work and labor until evening, giving that closing edge an ordinary workday scene.

column5: Prayer at evening, morning, and noon
column6: The commentary pairs devotion at the day's two edges; the psalmist says he prays at evening, morning, and noon, extending the pattern into a full daily cycle.

column5: Praise in morning and night
column6: The commentary hears the day's beginning and close together; the psalm appoints praise of steadfast love in the morning and faithfulness at night, a daily liturgical counterpart.

column5: Prayer as evening offering
column6: The commentary names the afternoon prayer and the day's closing edge; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense and raised hands like an evening offering, joining prayer to the late-day rite.

column5: Prayer times bounded by afternoon and evening
column6: The commentary notes that asr can name the afternoon prayer; the Mishnah sets the afternoon prayer's time until evening, placing a daily prayer within the same shrinking daylight boundary.

column5: Isaac's evening meditation read as afternoon prayer
column6: The commentary leaves open whether asr is the afternoon hour or a wider span of time; the Talmud derives the afternoon prayer from Isaac going out to meditate toward evening, giving that hour a Jewish interpretive tradition.

column5: Prayer at the ninth hour
column6: The commentary includes the afternoon prayer among possible senses of asr; Acts places Peter and John at the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer, showing a Christian practice at a named late-day hour.

column5: Alms and prayers remembered
column6: The commentary describes the squeezed extract as generosity flowing outward; the angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and alms have risen as a memorial, linking devotional practice with concrete giving.

column5: Third, sixth, and ninth-hour prayer
column6: The commentary names a fixed afternoon prayer within the day; Tertullian recognizes third, sixth, and ninth hours as customary times for prayer, showing a Christian daily rhythm that includes the closing daylight hours.

column5: Daily offerings at morning and twilight
column6: The commentary pairs the day's edges and names the afternoon prayer; Exodus assigns one lamb to morning and another to twilight, a daily ritual cycle ending as daylight closes.

column5: Rain waters furrows and blesses growth
column6: The commentary traces rain from squeezed clouds to grain and plants; the psalm describes God watering furrows with showers and blessing their growth, a close rain-to-crop sequence.

column5: The year crowned with abundance
column6: The commentary lets asr name both a day-part and a long age, then links time to yield; the psalm says God crowns the year with goodness, joining a temporal cycle to its harvest.

column5: Rain fills threshing floors and vats
column6: The commentary's squeezed-cloud image leads to grain, plants, and gardens; Joel describes threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing after rain, a parallel chain from water to agricultural abundance.

column5: Winepress as judgment
column6: The commentary's pressing can yield a gift or leave a dry remainder; Joel summons the sickle and treading of a full winepress as the nations' judgment, making the same harvest image destructive.

column5: The divine warrior treads the winepress alone
column6: The commentary distinguishes the flowing extract from the dry residue; Isaiah pictures God treading the winepress until garments are stained with blood, a counter-image in which pressing signifies judgment rather than bounty.

column5: The earth's vintage cast into God's winepress
column6: The commentary's grape pressing may stand for a good yield; Revelation gathers the earth's vintage and casts it into the winepress of divine wrath, giving the harvest image an apocalyptic judgment sense.

column5: Blood flows from the winepress
column6: The commentary describes pressing as separating liquid from dry pulp; Revelation says blood flows from the trampled winepress, turning that flow into a measure of catastrophic judgment.

column5: A rich man counts on many years of stored goods
column6: The commentary's garden owner has a final crop and an aging life; Luke's rich farmer stores abundant produce and assumes many years ahead, making stored yield a wager on future time.

column5: The future ends that night
column6: The commentary's old orchard owner loses the one harvest on which he depends; God tells Luke's farmer his life is required that very night, making the end of time arrive before expected use of stored goods.

column5: A great wind kills the children in a collapsing house
column6: The commentary's garden is destroyed by a whirlwind while its owner has weak descendants; Job reports a wind that collapses a house onto his children, a specific parallel of destructive wind and vulnerable offspring.

column5: A plant briefly shelters a distressed person
column6: The commentary calls asr a refuge for the distressed; Jonah's plant grows to shade him from discomfort, giving shelter a temporary, living form that can soon be lost.

column5: God as refuge in trouble
column6: The commentary calls the refuge a haven for a person in distress; the psalm names God as refuge and strength, a help in trouble, matching the concrete relation of shelter to pressure.

column5: Children have a refuge
column6: The commentary says lineage can be a place of refuge; Proverbs says the children of one who fears the Lord have refuge, directly joining descent and protection.

column5: Faith as a protective shield
column6: The commentary links refuge to armor that wraps and protects the body; Paul describes the shield of faith extinguishing flaming arrows, giving the protective covering an ethical and spiritual use.

column5: Testing produces endurance
column6: The commentary describes time's pressure as extracting an essence and connects the surah's final patience to a bitter extract; James says tested faith produces endurance, a specific ethical parallel between trial and patient strength.

column5: The delayed bridegroom and sleeping waiters
column6: The commentary includes late arrival and a sleep that may last only a moment; Matthew's bridegroom is delayed and the waiting women all grow sleepy and sleep, placing delay and sleep inside a story about readiness.

column5: The door closes before the late arrivals
column6: The commentary warns that work left undone near day's end may run out of time; Matthew's late bridesmaids arrive after the door is shut, making delay a lost opportunity.

column5: Menstruation as a timed ritual boundary
column6: The commentary's lexicon describes the first menstruating girl as held at home for protection; Leviticus assigns menstrual bleeding a seven-day impurity and contact rules, offering a distinct ritual reading of that timed threshold rather than confirming the commentary's protective etymology.

column5: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The package table gives Hebrew עצר a festival-assembly sense; Leviticus marks the eighth day with a sacred assembly, a calendrical use alongside the commentary's afternoon prayer and day-boundary senses, without establishing cognacy.

column5: A day and a thousand years
column6: The commentary holds the long age and short day-part together; Second Peter applies the psalm's thousand-years-as-a-day scale to the apparent delay of the Lord's coming, making divine and human time differ.

column5: Delay as time for repentance
column6: The commentary includes the sense of a late arrival and the dwindling time left to act; Second Peter interprets apparent delay as patience that gives people time to repent, turning lateness into mercy.

column5: Life as a mist that appears briefly
column6: The commentary lets asr range from a long era to a fleeting instant; James calls human life a mist that appears briefly and vanishes, a precise but less developed image of life's short span.

column5: Arabic ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary links its final word ṣabr, patience, to a bitter tree extract and to waiting through lean years while grain is saved; Genesis says Joseph heaped grain in extraordinary quantity. The table's ص ب ر / צבר match is only an unverified sound correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

column6: The commentary gives the Arabic dictionary sense of al-ʿaṣr as holding or detaining; Manoah asks to detain his visitor while preparing food, using Hebrew עצר. The package table marks the sound match as a candidate only.

column6: The commentary includes late or slow arrival and the sense of being held back; the Shunammite tells her servant not to slow her journey to Elisha, using Hebrew עצר. This is a precise semantic echo but the table does not verify cognacy.

column6: The commentary connects holding tightly with refuge and protection; Aaron stands between the dead and living while the plague is stopped with Hebrew עצר, a protective restraint that echoes that image.

column6: The commentary links squeezed rain clouds to grain and plants; Deuteronomy uses Hebrew עצר for shutting the heavens so rain and crop fail, a relevant withholding sense, though the root match remains unverified.

column6: The commentary contrasts rain that flows from clouds with a dry, pressed remnant; Job says that when God holds back waters they dry up, and when he releases them they flood the land, a close semantic fit through the table's unverified sound correspondence.
